newsitem.title: GERMANY: German managers to pay for broken promises.
newsitem.headline: German managers to pay for broken promises.

text.p: Germany's elite managers could once be secure in the belief that, even if their company wasn't quite hitting profit targets, the support of a few large, friendly shareholders meant their jobs were never on the line.

But now, with an influx of non-German investors gradually undoing the web of cross-holdings on which German business has traditionally been built, bosses are having to compete more fiercely for finance by offering promises of lucrative returns.
And those who fail to live up to those promises can expect short shrift from less sympathetic, internationally-minded investors, German finance experts said on Tuesday.

"If a manager promises a certain return rate and then, over two or three years, he doesn't produce it, nowadays he's got a serious problem," said Hans Peter Wodniok, German analyst at the Frankfurt office of Credit Lyonnais.

Such an analysis is perhaps too harsh in the case of Heyo Schmiedeknecht, who on Monday was forced to resign as head of engineering group Deutsche Babcock AG after it plunged to 1995/96 losses that he had at least managed to forecast.

But Schmiedeknecht, who had been blamed for taking Babcock on a disastrous spending spree that led ultimately to the losses, was nonetheless a victim of the greater demands being placed on German firms by shareholders, Wodniok believes.

"Shareholders aren't as easy to keep sweet as they were once. In the case of Babcock, I think shareholders began to worry that the outlook for this year looked pretty bad and in the end said: 'Let's get rid of him,'".

Although officially Schmiedeknecht resigned, it is widely believed that his days were numbered from the moment when Westdeutsche Landesbank (WestLB), holder of a significant minority stake, finally lost patience with him.

The fact that Babcock was immediately able to name a successor, ITT Automotive Europe head Klaus Lederer, supports the view that Schmiedeknecht was pushed out rather than exited of his own accord, observers note.
Such shareholder putsches are expected to become more frequent as German banks begin unravelling their substantial stakes in domestic companies to seek higher returns in international markets.

Some German managers -- notably Juergen Schrempp at industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG -- have sought to pre-empt the increased demands of investors by seeking to demonstrate a commitment to delivering "shareholder value".

But a study published late last year by Alfred Rappaport, the man credited with founding the shareholder value concept, showed that top German companies were still on average offering a paltry pay-back compared to a U.S. blue chip.

While only six of Germany's top 15 firms could deliver 15,000 marks today on a 10,000 mark investment made in 1986, U.S. equity returns on a $10,000 investment ranged from $24,000 to $131,000, Rappaport found.

Andrew Lockhart, German analyst at Robert Fleming in Frankfurt, said that more top-level executive victims could be expected as German companies began, with greater or lesser success, to tackle their bottom lines.
"It's going to be an uphill struggle and it will no doubt be accompanied by more news of corporate management changes," he said.

But he noted that a number of German companies had already moved fast to make the cost-cutting necessary to secure greater returns and some -- notably engineering firm Mannesmann AG with its mobile telecom business -- were already established in new high-growth markets.
"It shows that German management, once it has made up its mind, can actually come up with the goods," he said.
